stories.title: Africa: Are Bilateral Ties the Route to Renewed West African Security Cooperation?
stories.summary: Africa: Are Bilateral Ties the Route to Renewed West African Security Cooperation? 22 October 2026 Institute for Security Studies (Tshwane/Pretoria) analysis By Djiby Sow Pending the outcome of ECOWAS-AES talks, cooperation between neighbouring states offers a starting point for rebuilding regional security ties. Despite tensions between the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the Confederation of Sahel States (AES), recent advances reflect a broader regional trend. In August, Ghana and Burkina Faso signed a defence agreement , while Mali and Côte d'Ivoire agreed to delimit their shared border. The withdrawal of Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger from ECOWAS in January 2025 deeply fragmented West Africa's institutional architecture, but did not end cooperation between individual states. Instead, relations are being pragmatically reorganised around countries' security priorities, mainly through bilateral deals.

stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, There are no quick Ebola tests available to check travellers, so officials rely on monitoring temperatures By Makuochi Okafor ,Â BBC Africa Â and Â Simi Jolaoso ,Â Africa correspondent ,Â Reporting from Lagos Published 21 October 2026 Updated 1 hour ago Nigeria's first confirmed case of Ebola since the outbreak in East Africa began in May is the wife of a diplomat who travelled to Uganda's capital for a holiday, the head of Africa's health agency has told the BBC. The woman is originally from Uganda but based in Abuja, where she fell ill three days after arriving home in the Nigerian capital on 3 October, according to Dr Jean Kaseya from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. Nigeria's health minister has confirmed to the BBC the 42-year-old patient spent two and a half weeks in Kampala, adding that she also made a two-hour stopover in Ethiopia's capital on her return. "She's stable, she's improving," Muhammad Ali Pate said. The authorities were working to prevent the virus from spreading and had identified 44 people who had been in contact with the woman, who tested positive for Ebola on Tuesday, the minister said. stories.summary: Burkina Faso Restores Death Penalty Â© RFI Burkina Faso. 21 October 2026 Human Rights Watch (Washington, DC) By Ilaria Allegrozzi Chilling Message to Junta Critics Amid Sweeping Crackdowns Burkina Faso 's unelected parliament has unanimously adopted a new penal code that restores the death penalty for high treason, terrorism, acts of espionage, parricide and importation of expired or prohibited products. The country had abolished the death penalty for ordinary crimes in 2018 while its last known judicial execution took place in 1988. Reinstating capital punishment sends a chilling message to critics of the military junta and risks becoming another tool to suppress dissent. Since the September 2022 military coup , Burkina Faso's junta has steadily dismantled civic and political rights. Authorities have banned media outlets , suspended unions and civil society organizations , abolished multiparty politics , and subjected critics to arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances , unlawful conscription , and torture .

Africa has for decades been a transit point for Latin American cocaine making its way to European markets. The explosion in demand for cocaine and synthetic stimulants (notably methamphetamine), coupled with growing interdiction efforts in the Western Hemisphere, has resulted in a significant scaling up of Latin American cartel operations in Africa in recent years. stories.title: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
stories.summary: Image source, MSF via Reuters Image caption, Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town has been treating people wounded in Monday's attack on the market By Richard Kagoe ,Â Lucy Fleming Â and Â Richard Irvine-Brown ,Â BBC Verify Published 20 October 2026 Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral. The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 153 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said. A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF. The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011.

stories.title: Swimmer, 65, killed in shark attack off South Africa's east coast
stories.summary: Image source, Lochrenberg family Image caption, Janine Lochrenberg had "a deep affinity with the water" her sister told the BBC By Ed Habershon Reporting from Johannesburg Published 20 October 2026 A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year. Janine Lochrenberg was swimming off a beach in KuGompo City (formerly East London) on Tuesday morning when she was attacked. Witnesses said the 65-year-old was bitten in two places and died before she was brought to shore. Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal ones since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File. Lochrenberg was out on a daily morning swim with her local open water swimming club when she was attacked at around 08:00 (06:00 GMT).

stories.title: 'Tinubu Must Go!': Nigeria's northern protests test limits of political dissent
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5OTCD Police said the men were found in possession of 'dried leaves,' a pair of scissors and T-shirts bearing the phrase 'Tinubu Must Go!' Image: Borno State Police Command Advertisement T-shirts bearing the slogan "Tinubu Must Go!" — a reference to Nigerian President Bola Tinubu — are at the center of an escalating crackdown on dissent in Nigeria 's vast north. In September, police in the northeastern state of Borno arrested five men, aged between 21 and 44, over the shirts. Authorities have alleged the group had conspired to produce and wear them with the intention of breaching public peace. The men were subsequently charged with criminal conspiracy, inciting disturbance, disturbance of public peace and thuggery. Drawing criticism from human rights groups and activists, police later explained that the arrests followed a routine patrol and that officers had found substances believed to be illicit drugs and other items on the men, arguing that they were not being prosecuted for expressing their political views.

stories.title: Kenya cult leader's children still being starved weeks before trial, son says
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Paul Mackenzie said education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil" By Basma El Atti Reporting from Nairobi Published 20 October 2026 The eldest son of Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie, convicted of murdering 191 people, says his younger siblings were still being forced to fast as recently as two weeks ago. Dan Mackenzie, 27, said he reported the case to police, who rescued eight children, including his five younger siblings from their grandmother's house, and took them to a rescue centre. "They were basically forcibly fasted because they were denying food to them for almost three days," he tells BBC's Newsday. His father was found guilty on Monday of murdering 190 children and one adult who starved to death in Shakahola forest, near the Kenyan coast. He had ordered members of his doomsday cult to starve themselves and their children to death so they could "meet Jesus". Twenty-eight other cult leaders were also convicted of murder.

stories.title: Africa: African Development Bank Group Advances Sustainable Financing for Transboundary Waters At Iwc11 in Bali
stories.summary: African Development Bank Group Advances Sustainable Financing for Transboundary Waters At Iwc11 in Bali 20 October 2026 Content from a Premium Partner African Development Bank (Abidjan) announcement WHAT: African Development Bank Group participation at the 11th Global Environment Facility (GEF) Biennial International Waters Conference (IWC11) WHO: African Development Bank Group WHEN: 17-22 October 2026 WHERE: Anvaya Beach Resort, Bali, Indonesia The African Development Bank Group is participating in the 11th Global Environment Facility (GEF) Biennial International Waters Conference (IWC11), bringing its experience in financing sustainable development to global discussions on the future of transboundary waters and shared marine and freshwater ecosystems. IWC11 is taking place in Bali, Indonesia from 17 - 22 October 2026 under the theme "Shared Waters, Transformative Solutions: Enabling Systems Change." A key focus of the Bank's engagement will be sustainable financing. On 17 October, the Bank co-hosted the pre-conference workshop "From GEF Grants to Sustainable Investments: Financing the Future of Transboundary Waters and Shared Ecosystems," alongside the International Waters Learning Exchange and Resource Network (GEF IW:LEARN), the Asian Development Bank, the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, the Inter-American Development Bank and the World Bank. The workshop explored practical ways to move GEF International Waters projects beyond reliance on grant funding towards sustainable public and private investment, including blended finance and financing from multilateral development banks. During the workshop, the Bank Group led practical sessions on financing the transition to sustainable fisheries and aquaculture.

stories.title: Fleeing the frontline: Yemeni families cross Red Sea to Djibouti as Houthi conflict rages
stories.summary: Madinah Abdullah (in pink) and her family members at the Markazi humanitarian site in Obock, Djibouti, on 6 October. Photograph: Carlos Mureithi/The Guardian Their overland routes to safety blocked off, several thousand people have boarded boats to escape gunfire, bombing and a dire humanitarian situation By Carlos Mureithi in Obock A bubaker Saeed was fishing in the Red Sea off Yemen’s coast last month when he noticed explosions in the distance. His mind turned immediately to his wife and two children, and he raced back to his home village of al-Wahijah. Aircraft from the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemeni government forces had launched airstrikes in surrounding areas, targeting members of the Iran-aligned Houthi militia as its fighters approached the nearby port city of Mocha. “They were bombing Houthis while Houthis were 1km away from us,” the 50-year-old recalled. By the time he reached the shore, the rebels had arrived and were battling government forces on the ground.

stories.title: Africa: MDB Heads Strengthen Joint Action in Manila to Deliver More Financing and Greater Impact
stories.summary: MDB Heads Strengthen Joint Action in Manila to Deliver More Financing and Greater Impact 17 October 2026 Content from a Premium Partner African Development Bank (Abidjan) The Heads of Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs) Group met at the Asian Development Bank (ADB) headquarters in Manila today to discuss how to deliver more financing and greater impact to support developing members as they face mounting challenges. It was the Group's first-ever meeting in the Philippines, hosted by ADB as its 2026 Chair. "Conflict, economic uncertainty, high debt, inflation and disasters are placing growing pressure on our members and making development harder," said ADB President Masato Kanda, host and current Chair of the MDB Heads Group . "Our meeting in Manila was an opportunity to turn shared commitments into practical action, so we can help members protect their development gains, attract investment, and build more resilient economies." Against a backdrop of disasters, conflicts, difficult macroeconomic conditions, and constrained fiscal space, the Heads reaffirmed MDBs' readiness to provide timely financial and analytical support to protect vulnerable populations and sustain investment in jobs and resilient long-term growth. In a joint statement, the Heads welcomed the significant progress achieved this year working as a system to mobilize private capital, and on joint actions to advance jobs, nature, climate, water, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and other common development priorities, and on efforts to enhance system efficiency for greater impact at scale, in line with each institution's mandate, strategy and operational model. The role of Chair of the Heads of MDBs Group will be passed in December from ADB to the European Investment Bank Group. The Heads of MDBs Group includes the African Development Bank Group, Asian Development Bank, Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, Council of Europe Development Bank, European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, European Investment Bank Group, Inter-American Development Bank Group, Islamic Development Bank, New Development Bank, and the World Bank Group.

stories.title: Morocco's first female prime minister caught between the king, clerics, and feminists
stories.summary: Image source, Reuters Image caption, El Mansouri (left) was named by King Mohammed VI (right) as the country's first female prime minister By Basma El Atti Published 20 October 2026 The Islamic saying "a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed" has resurfaced in Morocco since King Mohammed VI named Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister. Mustafa Ramid, a former justice minister in an Islamist-led government, cited the saying earlier this month, in a lengthy Facebook post questioning whether a woman should hold the country's highest political office. He argued that Morocco, a Muslim majority country, had found a balance between equality and the responsibilities of state leadership, as the highest office - that of the king - continued to be reserved for men. Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy. Yet executive power remains in the hands of the 63-year-old monarch.

stories.title: Cameroun : Hemley Boum, « Nos vies sauvages » raconte un pays sous emprise
stories.summary: Que fait un pouvoir qui dure plus de quatre décennies à un pays et à ses habitants ? Dans son nouveau roman Nos vies sauvages, paru chez Gallimard, l'écrivaine camerounaise Hemley Boum raconte les destins de femmes confrontées à la corruption, à la répression et aux compromissions politiques. Un roman qui résonne avec l'histoire du Cameroun, de ses luttes pour l'indépendance à la présidentielle contestée de 2025. Sur France 24, Hemley Boum revient sur le système politique camerounais, la responsabilité des élites, les espoirs démocratiques déçus et les perspectives d'un changement après Paul Biya.

Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian Style of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowds By Eromo Egbejule in Lagos F or the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the University of Lagos, their classmate’s first-semester presentation was so captivating that they began calling him Toby Shang, after the 16th-century Chinese dynasty he had focused on. His crowd engagement that day had been harnessed from his high school days as a ginger-man (energiser) in a three-man band and as a private tutor. By his final year at university, his viral catchphrases and infectious energy had resulted in a hit song, Shedibalabala. Victoria would go on to pay for Bonetta’s education, approve her marriage to one of west Africa’s wealthiest men, and become godmother to her eldest daughter. stories.title: The Bundestag has debated the genocide Germany carried out in Namibia a century ago. But will it spur progress on addressing colonial crimes?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5OL1o Gaob David Timotheus Frederick (left) and Mutjinde Katjiua visited Germany this week to demand recognition and restitution Image: Christian Ditsch/epd Advertisement Gaob Daniel Timotheus Frederick was sitting in the front row of the visitors' gallery in the Bundestag this week. Wearing a suit and hat, he had traveled all the way from Namibia to see this parliamentary debate unfold. For almost 120 years, his family had been waiting for the return of human remains of their ancestor, Cornelius Frederick (sometimes spelled Fredericks), who had led the Nama resistance against German colonial rule and died on Shark Island in Germany's first concentration camp . In the name of his great-grandfather and as a member of the Nama Traditional Leaders Association (NTLA), Frederick was there to demand an "unconditioned apology" from Germany. Sitting next to him, in uniform and white gloves, with a carved lion on the handle of his walking stick, was the head of the Ovaherero Traditional Authority, Paramount Chief Mutjinde Katjiua.
